A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Moto study. The complete main text, supplementary Sections 7–10, equations, figures and tables support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original SIMPLER, CALVIN and real-world robot experiments, along with motion-token analyses and supplementary prediction results.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experiments and analyses, including benchmark results in Tables 2–3 and supplementary prediction accuracies in Table 8.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2–3.4 retain the same motion tokenizer, autoregressive Moto-GPT pre-training, action-query co-fine-tuning, attention masking and training losses.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same OXE/RT-1 data, CALVIN ABC-to-D setting, SSV2 human videos and three FANUC manipulation tasks, including novel-object and visual-distractor scenarios.

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 retain identical comparator sets, including both OpenVLA variants and the same CALVIN baselines. Figure 12 and Section 7.3 also retain the same Moto ablation variants.

E3.justification: Sections 4 and 7–8 retain the same splits, preprocessing, model configurations, training budgets and evaluation procedures, including 1,000 CALVIN task chains and 10 trials per real-world task.

E4.justification: The interpretability, trajectory-rationality, human-to-robot transfer, robustness, data-efficiency and co-fine-tuning analyses are unchanged. Supplementary reconstruction and trajectory-prediction examples are also retained.

E5.justification: Both retain likelihood averaging over 98 trajectory triplets and identical shaded bands in Figure 7. No run-count, seed, uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing information is added or revised.

E6.justification: Numerical and qualitative results match throughout. Moto retains 0.614 overall SIMPLER success in Table 2 and 3.10 average CALVIN task-chain length in Table 3. Supplementary Table 8 and Figures 15–16 are unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and objectives, including Equations 1–3, are unchanged. Neither version adds formal assumptions, propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same claims about motion-token representation, learning motion priors from videos and transferring those priors to robot control.

C2.justification: The interpretations of motion transfer, data efficiency and co-fine-tuning remain identical. Section 10 retains the same limitations and proposed extensions to broader video data and robotic tasks.

D1.justification: Sections 7–8 and Tables 4–7 retain identical implementation details, hyperparameters, GPU requirements, training durations and video-sampling instructions. The project access information is unchanged.

R1.justification: The same 62 references and related-work discussion are retained, including positioning against Genie, LAPO, DynaMo, LAPA and IGOR. Reference pagination changes without changes to cited works.

P1.justification: v4 revises Yi Chen's affiliation marker, adds a Tencent internship footnote, corrects Berkeley's affiliation number and adds a funding acknowledgement before the references. The scientific prose and section organization remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The added footnote slightly reflows the first page, and the acknowledgement shifts references across pages 9–12. Figures 1–16 and Tables 1–8 retain their content, structure and placement.

improvement.justification: v4 clarifies affiliation and funding attribution, with minor accompanying layout changes. The methods, empirical evidence, scientific explanations, limitations and reproducibility information remain unchanged, so these editorial refinements do not meaningfully alter overall paper quality.
